chapter: The 1949 band, breakup and later years
title: Walking out at Bop City and breaking his soprano
summary: Provoked by a singers' dispute and drinking, Barnet stopped the band in mid-opener, broke his soprano over his knee and flew home, returning five days later as if nothing had happened.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong

blocks.x: came up with a pretty fair band. Johnny Markham playing drums and a good tenor saxophone player from up north whose name escapes me. And Ray was there and it was his generalship in the trumpet section, and he took some of the guys that were there and got them together pretty good. Al Porsino joined the band. And by the time we got to New York it was a pretty respectable band. And we went in and played Bop City and that's when I pulled my thing. I got in a bind with a wife of mine, and on top of that I had a boy singer by the name of Bill Derry, who was a great singer in the Eckstine vein band. He was a white man, but he had a great deep voice and he did all of Billie's tunes, and he did them well. And there was another singer on the bill. I can't even remember this clown's name, if you want to know. He used to sing out of the side of his mouth. I don't know if that brings back -- he had gotten one hit record or something. Anyway, his manager - - Bill Derry was killing him, you know, and his manager pulled this,he said, "Does Bill Derry belong to the union?" I said, "What union?" He said, "Well, he may be a singer with the band, but if he works in New York he's got to belong to --," AFTRA or something. Well, the result was they were going to pull Bill from the show because he was hurting this other guy, you know. He was a better singer than he was. So I don't know, I was drinking and I flipped, and I walked out, we started to play the opening number and I absolutely flipped. I walked out in the middle of the stage in Bop City

and I stopped the band. I said, "I've been wanting to do this all my life. You can all go fuck yourselves." And I took my soprano and I broke it over my knee and walked out of the club, downstairs, and got in a taxicab and went to the airport and took a plane to California. Now, that is exactly what happened.
Wow. Did the band finish the engagement?

They kept the band. The band was playing, and then five days later, the hardest thing I ever had to do in my life. I walked in there and -- oh they were -- now they're scared, these hoods that had that joint, you know. They said, "Will he sue us? Will he sue us?" They figured I'd had a nervous breakdown, which I guess I did in a way, but it wasn't serious, you know, it was just a flipola. But they were scared I was going to sue them. Because I had fought them. I didn't want to play the place, you know, and they knew that. And they figured that they had caused this upheaval. So the hardest thing I ever had to do in my life, Pat, was like five days later I got on the plane and walked back there, and I walked in right before the show and I walked backstage like nothing has happened and just took over where I left off. Never said a word to the band. The band never said a word to me, and we finished the engagement. And these guys never said a word to me.

In the meantime, I had a valet who had been with me for like 18 years, Curry Wilson, what a doll. He had gone out and he had gotten the horn repaired. He got it all straightened out and everything, all the keys put back on, because it was a mess. I really -- it was bow-shaped, and I had a big bruise on my knee. They're pretty hard, you know, those sopranos.
But you felt better. This is really going back, but you felt better after you did it, didn't you?
I don't know. It had to happen. It had to happen. Something had to happen. Something awful had to happen. I'm glad it was that way, I didn't hurt somebody or something, you know.
